strengths: Addresses a clear and practical gap: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for wide field-of-view cameras, including fisheye and 360-degree imagery, without requiring explicit rectification.

The combination of a spherical-harmonics ray representation with a camera model token within a multi-view permutation-equivariant architecture is a sensible and well-motivated design for distortion-aware reconstruction.
Strong empirical results are reported across multiple tasks and datasets, with particularly large improvements on 360-degree settings such as Stanford2D3D, where pinhole baselines degrade sharply.

The experimental section is broad, covering zero-shot pose estimation, point map estimation, large-scale localization, monocular 360 depth estimation, and ablations on training data composition, camera tokens, and batch-frame count.

Training data and augmentation strategies are thoughtfully assembled, including fisheye-from-pinhole augmentation and equirectangular rotation augmentation, which support learning across diverse camera models.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear architecture overview and useful qualitative visualizations of reconstruction and localization results.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the spherical-harmonics ray representation and asymmetric ray loss closely follow UniK3D, the multi-view permutation-equivariant backbone follows pi3, and camera-model conditioning is related to prior calibration-token approaches. The main contribution is primarily a system-level integration and extension to multi-view wide-FoV settings.

The camera model token is under-specified. The paper does not define how tokens are constructed, how many exist, how they are injected into the network, or how they behave under unknown, misclassified, or continuously varying camera models. Inference still appears to require knowledge of the camera type, which weakens the claim of operating without calibration.

Evaluation fairness is a concern. Baselines such as VGGT and pi3 are pinhole-oriented methods run directly on distorted wide-FoV images. A critical missing comparison is undistortion/rectification followed by the same pinhole baselines (or fine-tuned baselines), which would isolate the benefit of the proposed architecture from simply avoiding rectification.

Potential training/test overlap is not adequately clarified. Matterport3D and ScanNet++ appear in the training data but are also used in point map and localization evaluations. This makes some results non-zero-shot for those datasets and raises questions about fair comparison to baselines that may not have seen the same data.

Some claims are overstated. The conclusion states 'superior accuracy in monocular depth estimation,' but in Table 6 Wid3R is worse than several specialized monocular 360 methods in Abs Rel and RMSE, and only competitive on delta thresholds. The large-scale localization section also says 3D maps are produced 'within three seconds' while Table 4 lists a runtime of 50 for Wid3R, creating an inconsistency.

Reproducibility details are insufficient. The paper lacks key hyperparameters and design choices such as spherical-harmonics order L, token dimensionality, feature aggregation details, batch sizes, number of training iterations, and whether code will be released.

Ablation Table 7 is difficult to parse and does not thoroughly analyze several important factors, including sensitivity to spherical-harmonics order, camera-token type/definition, robustness to unseen fisheye distortion, use of the uncertainty output, and computational cost at inference.

The paper does not evaluate on unknown or continuous camera models, dynamic scenes beyond a brief limitation note, or outdoor wide-FoV settings, which limits confidence in real-world generalizability. Table formatting and reference issues (e.g., 'SPSS [20.22]', 'EDM [31] + DSSM [31]') further hinder clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for wide field-of-view imagery such as fisheye and 360° cameras.

Combines established strong components (π3-style permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone, UniK3D-style ray/spherical-harmonic representation, and camera-model conditioning) into a unified pipeline.
Evaluates on a broad set of datasets and tasks, including zero-shot pose estimation, point map reconstruction, monocular 360° depth, and large-scale localization.
Reports strong empirical gains in several settings, especially for 360° point map reconstruction and pose estimation relative to pinhole-focused baselines.
Includes ablation studies on camera tokens, training data composition, and number of frames per batch.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing π3 architecture, UniK3D ray representation, and a simple discrete camera token. The camera token only distinguishes pinhole/fisheye/360° and cannot capture camera-specific intrinsics or distortion parameters, so the claimed 'camera model conditioning' is much weaker than presented.

The core ray representation is insufficiently specified and in places technically unclear. Eq. (8) defines ray directions via spherical-harmonic coefficients conditioned only on a camera token, but it is not explained how θ and φ are obtained for arbitrary distorted image pixels, nor whether the coefficients are per-pixel or per-image. As written, the formulation cannot reconstruct pixel-dependent ray directions for a general camera.

The loss formulation is unclear and contains apparent errors: L_points is referenced but never defined, Eq. (12) is garbled, the asymmetric ray loss in Eq. (9) has undefined quantities and likely typos, and the interaction between point, ray, radial, uncertainty, normal, and pose losses is not cleanly presented.

Experimental comparisons are not fully convincing. The main pose and point-map baselines (VGGT, π3) are pinhole-specific models and are not designed for wide FoV inputs, while no wide-FoV multi-view or 360° SfM/feed-forward baseline is included for those tasks. This makes the large reported gains less informative.

Evaluation details are incomplete and sometimes concerning: point-map metrics involve sequential Umeyama alignment, MoGe alignment, and ICP, but it is not clear whether this is applied identically to all methods or how much it contributes to the gains. RRA@30 = 100.0 on FIORD also warrants more scrutiny and protocol detail.

The ablation does not clearly support the stated conclusions. In Table 7, adding pinhole/fisheye data sometimes worsens mean accuracy, and frame-count results are mixed; the text claims consistent improvements that the numbers do not obviously demonstrate.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. For example, Table 4 shows lower AUC than EDM+DSSM or SPSG+COLMAP on several scenes despite the text claiming superior registration accuracy, and Table 6 does not show state-of-the-art monocular 360° depth performance despite the 'comparable or superior' framing.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or detailed architecture/training description is provided, dataset splits and sizes are vague, the camera-token implementation is unspecified, and key implementation choices (SH degree, ray module design, training schedule, use of pretrained π3 weights) are missing.

strengths: Targets an important and under-addressed problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction from wide field-of-view imagery, including fisheye and 360-degree cameras, where existing multi-view foundation models are largely pinhole-centric.

The proposed ray-based representation with spherical harmonics and camera model tokens is a sensible and effective design for distortion-aware geometry estimation without explicit undistortion or rectification.

The paper reports strong empirical gains across multiple tasks and datasets, especially zero-shot pose estimation and point map reconstruction on Stanford2D3D, Zip-NeRF, and FIORD, with large margins over VGGT and pi3.
It demonstrates the first feed-forward multi-view reconstruction directly from 360-degree imagery, which is a meaningful capability with practical impact for robotics, AR/VR, and large-scale mapping.

The experiments are broad, covering camera pose estimation, large-scale localization, point map estimation, monocular 360 depth estimation, and ablations on camera token conditioning and training data composition.
The ablation study provides useful evidence that training with diverse camera models improves 360-degree performance and reduces variance, despite the limited amount of 360-degree training data.
Feed-forward inference brings clear efficiency benefits over SfM-style pipelines, as shown qualitatively and quantitatively in the large-scale Matterport3D localization setting.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear problem formulation, architecture description, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines established components from pi3 (local point maps, permutation-equivariant design, pose head) and UniK3D (spherical-harmonics ray representation, asymmetric ray loss), with camera tokens being related to existing calibration-token ideas. The core contribution is their integration for multi-view wide-FoV reconstruction.

The method requires a known camera model token at inference. It is not fully clear how robust it is to unknown or incorrect camera model selection, or how the token should be chosen for real fisheye lenses with varying distortion parameters.

The ablation does not isolate the proposed spherical-harmonics angular module versus a standard point-map head, nor the decoupled angular/radial modules or uncertainty head. This weakens direct evidence for some architectural claims.

Training data for 360-degree cameras account for less than 1% of the total, and although the ablation is encouraging, stronger real-world evaluation across diverse 360-degree and fisheye sensors/intrinsics would better support generalization claims.

Baselines are evaluated on distorted wide-FoV images without undistortion or calibration, which matches the paper's setting but does not fully rule out stronger undistort-then-reconstruct pipelines as a fair comparison point.

The large-scale localization results are not consistently superior across all scenes; some AUC values are lower than dense matching baselines, so the claim of superior registration accuracy needs qualification.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity, including apparent typos such as pi3 appearing as x^2 in Table 5, garbled Equation 12, inconsistent Table 4 headers, and unclear units for the runtime column.

Reproducibility is somewhat limited: no code or model release is indicated, and details of training schedules, token definitions, and dataset preprocessing are not sufficiently specified for easy reproduction.

Point map evaluation depends on alignment procedures (Umeyama, MoGe, ICP), and the paper does not analyze how sensitive the reported numbers are to these choices or whether they could favor the proposed method.

strengths: Addresses an important open problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction directly from distorted fisheye/360° imagery without explicit undistortion.
Extends existing π3 and UniK3D ideas to multi-view wide-FOV reconstruction by introducing ray-based angular/radial modules and camera model conditioning.
Provides a broad empirical study across pose estimation, point map reconstruction, monocular depth, large-scale localization, and ablations over training data, camera tokens, and frame count.
Achieves strong gains in several settings, especially 360° point map and pose benchmarks, and shows very fast feed-forward localization compared with SfM-based pipelines.
Includes sensible design choices such as permutation-equivariant local coordinate frames, radial-distance-weighted scale alignment, overlap-based batch sampling, and camera augmentation.
Discusses limitations and future work, particularly regarding dynamic scenes.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely combines existing π3 permutation-equivariant multi-view architecture, UniK3D spherical-harmonic ray representation, and a token-conditioning mechanism. The main new component, camera model tokens, is closer to a conditioning trick than a fundamental advance.

The camera model token is under-specified and potentially misleading. It conditions on camera category (pinhole/fisheye/360°) rather than intrinsics or distortion parameters, yet the paper claims reconstruction without explicit calibration. There is no evaluation of mismatched or unknown camera tokens, varying focal lengths, or distortion parameter variation.

Equation 8 suggests the angular module’s SH coefficients depend only on the camera token, which would be insufficient to model per-camera intrinsics across datasets. If image features also condition the coefficients, this is not made clear; the architecture needs clarification.

Evidence that the ray-based modules are responsible for the gains is mixed. On FIORD, ‘Ours (π3)’ trained with the same wide-angle data outperforms ‘Ours (Wid3R)’ in AUC@30 and several trajectory-error metrics. Gains on other datasets may therefore reflect training data, augmentation, or token conditioning rather than the proposed ray representation.

Several experimental tables are difficult to parse and appear internally inconsistent. For example, normal consistency values above 1 and metric directions that seem to contradict the stated ‘higher/lower is better’ notation make the point-map and localization results hard to verify.

Comparisons are limited to VGGT and π3. Recent feed-forward or ray-based reconstruction methods such as Depth Anything 3 and MapAnything are cited but not experimentally compared, despite being highly relevant.

Point map evaluation on Matterport3D and ScanNet++ is in-domain, since those datasets are also used for training; the paper does not establish zero-shot generalization across truly unseen wide-angle cameras.

The ablation study is narrow: camera token use is only tested as present/absent, with no analysis of token selection, token robustness, or generalization to new camera models. The claim that diverse camera training uniformly improves 360° performance is only partially supported by the reported ablation numbers.
Monocular 360° depth results are described as ‘comparable or superior,’ but the method is worse than several specialized baselines in Abs Rel and RMSE, so the claim is overstated.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing code/details: no explicit data splits, no confidence intervals or seed variance, and insufficient clarity on how camera model tokens are assigned or how the method handles unknown camera types at test time.

The ‘first multi-frame feed-forward method supporting 360° imagery’ claim needs stronger literature positioning, especially given possible cubemap-based applications of existing feed-forward models and concurrent works.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for wide field-of-view cameras, including fisheye and 360° imagery.
The combination of a ray-based angular/radial representation with camera-type conditioning is sensible, and the overall system is built on strong recent backbones (π3, UniK3D, DINOv2).
The paper reports extensive experiments across several datasets and tasks, including pose estimation, point map reconstruction, large-scale localization, and monocular 360° depth estimation.
The claimed runtime advantage on large-scale Matterport3D localization (seconds vs. minutes for SfM pipelines) is practically relevant if validated.
The ablation study on camera-model tokens, training-data composition, and number of frames per batch provides some useful insight, especially regarding 360° data scarcity.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the ray-based spherical-harmonics representation and camera-token conditioning are heavily derived from prior work (UniK3D, calibration tokens), and the multi-view extension largely fine-tunes π3. The main contribution is an application/combination rather than a fundamentally new method.

The empirical evidence does not isolate the proposed modules convincingly. The “Ours (π3)” baseline, which only fine-tunes π3 on wide-angle data without ray modules or camera tokens, already achieves most of the reported gains over VGGT/π3. The ray modules and tokens improve results inconsistently; e.g., on FIORD pose estimation, “Ours (Wid3R)” is worse than “Ours (π3)” in AUC, ATE, and RPE trans.

Camera model conditioning requires knowing the correct camera-model token at test time, which is a form of explicit camera-type supervision. The paper does not evaluate robustness to an incorrect token, unseen camera models, or continuous distortions, so the “without explicit calibration” claim is overstated.

Several reported metrics and tables are inconsistent or unclear. For example, Table 5 lists N.C. values greater than 1 for some methods while marking N.C. as higher-is-better; Table 4 is garbled and hard to interpret; the abstract’s +77.33 gain does not exactly match Table 2. This raises concerns about the reliability of the experimental evidence.

Comparison protocols may be unfair or insufficiently controlled: zero-shot VGGT/π3 are compared to fine-tuned Wid3R on wide-angle training data, and there is no comparison to fine-tuned VGGT or other multi-view wide-angle baselines. Training/test overlap or contamination is not clearly discussed, especially since Matterport3D appears in both training and evaluation.
The monocular 360° depth results in Table 6 do not support the claim of superior accuracy; Wid3R is worse than several specialized methods (e.g., Depth Anywhere, ACDNet, Bifuse++) in Abs Rel.

Reproducibility is limited: details on the camera-token embeddings, token selection at inference, network architecture differences from π3/UniK3D, training schedule, compute cost, and code/weights availability are insufficient.

There is no direct evaluation of the ray representation itself, such as angular ray error, sensitivity to spherical-harmonic order, or uncertainty calibration. The uncertainty output is introduced but not meaningfully used or validated.

The ablation shows only modest gains from camera tokens, and the improvements from adding diverse camera data suggest that much of the performance comes from data and fine-tuning rather than the proposed architecture.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical gap: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for fisheye and 360° imagery without explicit undistortion or calibration.

The proposed ray-based representation with spherical harmonics and camera-model tokens is technically reasonable, builds effectively on π³ and UniK3D, and enables a unified architecture across pinhole, fisheye, and spherical cameras.

The paper presents a strong empirical study across multiple wide-FOV datasets, including zero-shot pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, monocular 360° depth estimation, and large-scale localization.
Large performance gains are reported on challenging 360° settings, e.g., Stanford2D3D pose and point-map metrics, where prior feed-forward methods degrade severely.
The ablation study provides useful evidence that training with diverse camera models improves generalization to 360° data and that camera-model tokens contribute positively.
The feed-forward formulation is highly efficient compared with SfM/bundle-adjustment pipelines for large-scale 360° localization, as shown by the reported runtime.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and transparent about limitations such as dynamic scenes.
weaknesses: The method is not fully calibration-free in practice: at inference one must still provide a camera-model token (pinhole/fisheye/360°), which assumes knowledge or estimation of the camera category. Robustness to unknown or mis-specified tokens is not evaluated.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: the approach combines existing components (π³-style permutation-equivariant multi-view reconstruction, UniK3D-style rays/spherical harmonics, and camera tokens) with relatively limited architectural innovation beyond conditioning.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the large-scale localization section states superior registration accuracy, but in Table 4 the EDM+IM360 baseline appears better on several AUC metrics; the main clear advantage is runtime.

The improvements are not uniformly consistent. For example, in FIORD pose evaluation, Ours (π³) has better AUC and ATE than the full Wid3R variant on some metrics, and in Matterport3D point-map accuracy the π³ variant is better on mean Acc.

Important reproducibility details are missing or relegated to the supplement, such as spherical-harmonic order L, camera-token vocabulary/dimension, training schedule, and exact implementation of token selection.

The ablation results are somewhat nuanced: adding fisheye data alone can worsen mean Acc on Stanford2D3D, so the conclusion that diverse camera training consistently improves performance requires more careful qualification.
No direct baseline compares against a cubemap/undistortion + perspective feed-forward pipeline, even though this is a natural practical alternative discussed in the supplementary material.
